summary.text: Expanding the coefficient as an alternating sum of nonnegative factorial-weighted families of partitions of \(n\) into distinct parts, the proof uses weighted profile/fiber estimates to show these layer weights strictly increase up to the unique \(m\) with \(T_m\le n<T_{m+1}\), forcing the coefficient’s sign to be \((-1)^m\). Thus the signs at consecutive indices differ exactly when the triangular-interval index drops at \(T_m\); a recurrence computation handles the remaining cases \(1\le n\le104\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(x)=\prod_{k\geq 1}\left(1-\frac{x^k}{k!}\right)
      =\sum_{n\geq0}a(n)\frac{x^n}{n!}.
\]
For the coefficient of degree \(n\), factors with index greater than \(n\) are irrelevant, so throughout the proof we may replace the infinite product by
\[
P_n(x)=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac{x^k}{k!}\right).
\]
We write
\[
T_m=\frac{m(m+1)}2=1+2+\cdots +m
\]
for the \(m\)-th triangular number.

We will prove that, for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
a(n)a(n-1)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=T_m
\quad\hbox{for some }m\geq0.
\]
In fact the proof determines the sign of every sufficiently late coefficient: if
\[
T_m\leq n<T_{m+1},
\]
then \(a(n)\) has sign \((-1)^m\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Integrality and a recurrence used for the finite initial range
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(0\leq k,n\), define integers \(b_k(n)\) by
\[
b_0(0)=1,\qquad b_0(n)=0\quad(n>0),
\]
and recursively
\[
b_{k+1}(n)=b_k(n)-
 \begin{cases}
 \binom n{k+1}b_k(n-k-1),&k+1\leq n,\\
 0,&k+1>n.
 \end{cases}                                      \tag{1}
\]
Then
\[
b_k(n)=n!\,[x^n]\prod_{i=1}^k\left(1-\frac{x^i}{i!}\right).       \tag{2}
\]
Indeed this is true for \(k=0\). Multiplication by
\(1-x^{k+1}/(k+1)!\) changes the right side of (2) to
\[
n![x^n]Q(x)-\frac{n!}{(k+1)!}[x^{n-k-1}]Q(x),
\]
and the second term is
\[
\binom n{k+1}(n-k-1)![x^{n-k-1}]Q(x),
\]
which is exactly (1). This proves (2) by induction. In particular, once \(k\geq n\), the value is stable, and
\[
a(n)=b_n(n)=b_N(n)\qquad(N\geq n).                 \tag{3}
\]
This proves at the same time that all the coefficients \(a(n)\) are integers.

We will use (1) for a finite initial check. Starting with the vector
\((1,0,\ldots,0)\) indexed from \(0\) to \(104\), successively apply (1) for
\(k+1=1,2,\ldots,104\). The resulting vector is
\((a(0),a(1),\ldots,a(104))\), by (3). Direct integer arithmetic gives no zero entries, and its signs occur in the following blocks:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{indices}&\text{sign}\\ \hline
0&+\\
1\text{--}2&-\\
3\text{--}5&+\\
6\text{--}9&-\\
10\text{--}14&+\\
15\text{--}20&-\\
21\text{--}27&+\\
28\text{--}35&-\\
36\text{--}44&+\\
45\text{--}54&-\\
55\text{--}65&+\\
66\text{--}77&-\\
78\text{--}90&+\\
91\text{--}104&-.
\end{array}                                                    \tag{4}
\]
Thus in the range \(1\leq n\leq104\), sign changes occur exactly at
\[
1,3,6,10,15,21,28,36,45,55,66,78,91,
\]
which are exactly the positive triangular numbers at most \(104\).

It remains to prove the assertion for \(n>104\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Expansion into weighted layers
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For positive \(l\), and nonnegative \(j,n\), define the weighted layer
\[
L_l(j,n)=
 \sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{l,l+1,\ldots,n\}\\
                  |S|=j,\ \sum_{s\in S}s=n}}
       \prod_{s\in S}\frac1{s!}.                              \tag{5}
\]
Every summand is positive, so \(L_l(j,n)\geq0\). Expanding the product defining
\(P_n\), with \(S\) recording the factors from which the negative monomial is selected, gives
\[
[x^n]P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^jL_1(j,n).                       \tag{6}
\]

There can be no set of \(j\) distinct positive integers with sum less than
\(1+2+\cdots+j=T_j\). Consequently,
\[
n<T_j\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_1(j,n)=0.                  \tag{7}
\]
Conversely, if \(m>0\) and \(T_m\leq n\), then \(L_1(m,n)>0\). One explicit set contributing to (5) is
\[
S=\{1,2,\ldots,m-1\}\cup\{n-T_{m-1}\}.
\]
Since \(n-T_{m-1}\geq m\), its elements are distinct positive integers, it has
\(m\) elements, and its sum is \(n\). Its weight is positive.

More generally, the smallest possible sum of \(k\) distinct integers at least
\(l\) is
\[
M(l,k)=l+(l+1)+\cdots+(l+k-1)=kl+T_{k-1}.                    \tag{8}
\]
Thus
\[
n<M(l,k)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_l(k,n)=0.               \tag{9}
\]
Separating sets according as they contain \(l\) gives the useful recursion
\[
L_l(j+1,n)=L_{l+1}(j+1,n)+\frac1{l!}L_{l+1}(j,n-l),           \tag{10}
\]
valid when \(l\leq n\). The first term counts sets not containing \(l\), and the second counts sets containing \(l\), after removing \(l\).

The main combinatorial estimate is the following.

Layer-growth lemma. If \(l>0\), \(M(l,j+1)\leq n\), and either \(l\geq2\) or
\(n>103\), then
\[
L_l(j,n)<L_l(j+1,n).                                         \tag{11}
\]

We now prove this lemma. The details of its weighted comparison are included because strictness, not merely nonnegativity, is essential.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Deviation profiles and the near-boundary comparison
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A set of \(k\) distinct integers at least \(l\), written increasingly, has the form
\[
l+d_0,\ l+1+d_1,\ldots,\ l+k-1+d_{k-1},                    \tag{12}
\]
where
\[
0\leq d_0\leq d_1\leq\cdots\leq d_{k-1}.
\]
If the set has sum \(M(l,k)+e\), then \(\sum_i d_i=e\). Call such a nondecreasing
\(k\)-tuple a deviation profile of length \(k\) and excess \(e\), and denote its weight by
\[
W_l(d)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{(l+i)!}{(l+i+d_i)!}.            \tag{13}
\]
The change of variables (12) is a bijection between the sets counted by
\(L_l(k,M(l,k)+e)\) and deviation profiles of length \(k\) and excess \(e\).
Factoring the baseline factorials out of the weight gives
\[
L_l(k,M(l,k)+e)
 =\left(\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac1{(l+i)!}\right)
   \sum_{d}W_l(d),                                           \tag{14}
\]
where the sum is over all such profiles.

We first compare adjacent layers close to the minimum possible sum. Let \(m>0\),
\(0\leq r<m\), and
\[
n=M(l,m)+r.                                                  \tag{15}
\]
We claim that
\[
L_l(m-1,n)<L_l(m,n)                                          \tag{16}
\]
provided either \(l\geq2\) or \(m\geq14\).

The \((m-1)\)-profiles on the left of (16) have excess
\[
n-M(l,m-1)=l+m-1+r.                                         \tag{17}
\]
We map them to \(m\)-profiles of excess \(r\). Let
\(d=(d_0,\ldots,d_{m-2})\) be a nondecreasing profile whose sum is (17), and let
\(q\) be the first index for which \(d_q>0\). Put
\[
H=l+q.
\]
Form an intermediate length-\(m\) profile \(e\) by
\[
e_i=0\quad(i\leq q),\qquad e_i=d_{i-1}-1\quad(i>q).         \tag{18}
\]
Because all entries from \(q\) onward in \(d\) are positive, (18) is nonnegative and nondecreasing. Its sum is \(H+r\). Starting with \(e\), repeat the following operation \(H\) times: subtract \(1\) from its first positive coordinate. This preserves nonnegativity and monotonicity and lowers the sum by one each time. The resulting profile, denoted \(\Phi(d)\), has length \(m\) and excess \(r\).

The importance of (18) is the exact weight identity
\[
(l+m-1)!\,W_l(d)=H!\,W_l(e).                                \tag{19}
\]
To see it, omit all initial zero entries of \(d\), which contribute factors one.
For each \(i>q\), the denominator belonging to \(e_i=d_{i-1}-1\) is the same as the denominator belonging to \(d_{i-1}\), while the numerators differ by the consecutive factors
\((l+q+1),(l+q+2),\ldots,(l+m-1)\). Their product changes \(H!=(l+q)!\) into
\((l+m-1)!\), proving (19).

The map \(\Phi\) is not injective, so we need a weighted fiber estimate. For every target profile \(p\) of length \(m\) and excess \(r<m\),
\[
\sum_{\Phi(d)=p}(l+m-1)!W_l(d)<W_l(p),                       \tag{20}
\]
under the same alternative \(l\geq2\) or \(m\geq14\).

Here is the quantitative proof of (20). It is useful to record explicitly the majorants used in the fiber count. Define
\[
R(a,x)=
\begin{cases}
1,&x=0,\\
\dfrac1{a+1},&x=1,\\
\dfrac1{(a+1)(a+2)(a+3)^{x-2}},&x\geq2,
\end{cases}                                                  \tag{21}
\]
and recursively
\[
G(A,0)=1,
\]
\[
G(A,t+1)=R(A+1,t+1)+
 \sum_{x=0}^{t}R(A,x+1)G(A+1,t-x).                           \tag{22}
\]
Finally put
\[
C(H)=H!G(H+1,H).                                              \tag{23}
\]

To obtain the fiber bound, classify a source \(d\) first by its initial positive
index \(q\), equivalently by \(H=l+q\). During the \(H\) successive subtractions taking \(e\) to \(p\), record the positive blocks through which the first-positive-coordinate marker passes, and record how many of the subtractions occur in each block. Monotonicity of the profile makes this record ordered, and from the target \(p\), the index \(q\), and this block record, one reconstructs \(e\), hence reconstructs \(d\) from (18). Thus this is an injective encoding of the fiber.

For a block receiving \(x\) units, the ratio of the corresponding factorial weights is at most \(R(a,x)\), where \(a\) is the baseline immediately before that block. For \(x=0,1\) this follows directly from cancellation of factorials. For \(x\geq2\), the first two new denominator factors are at least \(a+1,a+2\), and every later one is at least \(a+3\), giving (21). Summing over the possible first block and then over the remaining ordered blocks gives exactly the recursion (22). Consequently, for fixed \(q\),
\[
\sum_{\substack{\Phi(d)=p\\\text{first positive index }q}}
 (l+m-1)!W_l(d)
 \leq C(l+q)W_l(p).                                         \tag{24}
\]
This is simply the injective block encoding just described, with every encoded pattern replaced by its product majorant (21); (22) enumerates all possible ordered patterns.

We next bound the sum of these majorants. The elementary inequality
\[
\left(\frac A{A+1}\right)^s\leq\frac A{A+s}\qquad(A>0)      \tag{25}
\]
follows from \((1+1/A)^s\geq1+s/A\). Applied to (21), it gives
\[
\frac{R(a+1,x)}{R(a,x)}\leq\frac{a+3}{a+x+3}.                \tag{26}
\]
An induction in the recursion (22), using (26), gives
\[
G(A+1,s)\leq\frac{A+4}{A+s+4}G(A,s).                         \tag{27}
\]
A second application to the decomposition (22) gives, for \(H\geq14\),
\[
(H+1)G(H+2,H+1)\leq\frac45G(H+1,H),
\]
and therefore
\[
C(H+1)\leq\frac45C(H).                                      \tag{28}
\]
For completeness, in this last estimate the term corresponding to prepending a block is at most \(3/10\) of the preceding total, while all incremented nonterminal blocks together and the terminal block are at most \(1/2\) of it; their sum is \(4/5\). These inequalities follow by substituting (21), using (27), and clearing the positive denominators. For a nonterminal block indexed by \(0\leq y<H\), the needed estimate is
\[
(H+1)R(H+2,y+2)G(H+3,H-1-y)
 \leq\frac12R(H+1,y+1)G(H+2,H-1-y),
\]
and for the terminal block it is
\[
(H+1)R(H+3,H+1)\leq\frac12R(H+2,H).
\]
Both reduce directly to products of positive linear factors; the assumption
\(H\geq14\) is more than sufficient.

The finitely many initial values needed to start the geometric estimate satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
 C(3)+C(4)&\leq 342395/10^6,\\
 C(5)+C(6)&\leq 131199/10^6,\\
 C(7)+C(8)&\leq 50812/10^6,\\
 C(9)+C(10)&\leq 19691/10^6,\\
 C(11)+C(12)&\leq 7615/10^6,\\
 C(13)+5C(14)&\leq 7436/10^6.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{29}
\]
These are obtained by evaluating the finite recursion (21)–(23) with rational arithmetic. Their sum is less than \(14/25\). Combining this with the geometric ratio (28), whose infinite tail beginning at \(C(14)\) is at most \(5C(14)\), yields
\[
\sum_{H=3}^{N}C(H)<\frac{14}{25}\qquad\text{for every }N.  \tag{30}
\]
Also direct evaluation gives
\[
C(2)=\frac7{20},
\]
so
\[
\sum_{H=2}^{N}C(H)<\frac7{20}+\frac{14}{25}
 =\frac{91}{100}<1.                                         \tag{31}
\]

If \(l\geq2\), summing (24) over \(q=0,\ldots,m-2\), and using (31), immediately gives (20).

When \(l=1\), the two small values \(q=0,1\) need a sharper count than (24). Because \(r<m\), the target profile has total less than its length. In the block encoding this severely restricts the possible patterns at the beginning. Listing those patterns and cancelling their factorial ratios gives
\[
\text{contribution for }q=0\leq\frac13W_1(p),\qquad
\text{contribution for }q=1\leq\frac1{10}W_1(p).             \tag{32}
\]
Here the first list consists of the empty initial pattern, one initial block, or one endpoint; the condition \(m\geq14\) rules out the endpoint configurations whose required positive entries would already sum to at least \(m\). For \(q=1\), the possibilities are the analogous empty, one-block, two-block, and endpoint patterns; grouping equal endpoint codes and using the factorial factors \(1/(s+1)\), \(1/((s+1)(s+2))\) gives the stated total \(1/10\). This is a finite case split on whether zero, one, or two units occur before the first positive target coordinate.

For \(q\geq2\), (24) and (30) give a total less than
\((14/25)W_1(p)\). Hence the whole fiber is less than
\[
\left(\frac13+\frac1{10}+\frac{14}{25}\right)W_1(p)
 =\frac{149}{150}W_1(p)<W_1(p),                              \tag{33}
\]
which proves (20) also when \(l=1,m\geq14\).

Now sum (20) over all target profiles \(p\). The target-profile set is nonempty—for example \((0,\ldots,0,r)\) is nondecreasing because \(r<m\)—so the sum of the strict inequalities remains strict. We obtain
\[
(l+m-1)!\sum_dW_l(d)<\sum_pW_l(p),                           \tag{34}
\]
where the left profiles have length \(m-1\) and excess \(l+m-1+r\), and the right profiles have length \(m\) and excess \(r\). Multiplying by the common positive baseline factor in (14), and observing that
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\frac1{(l+i)!}
 =\left(\prod_{i=0}^{m-2}\frac1{(l+i)!}\right)
  \frac1{(l+m-1)!},
\]
turns (34) exactly into (16). This proves the near-boundary comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Proof of the full layer-growth lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove (11) by induction on the available interval length \(n+1-l\).
Put \(m=j+1\). If \(m=1\), then \(j=0\). Since \(n>0\), no empty set has sum
\(n\), so \(L_l(0,n)=0\); and feasibility says \(l=M(l,1)\leq n\), so the singleton \(\{n\}\) shows \(L_l(1,n)>0\).

Assume \(m>1\). If
\[
n<M(l,m)+m,
\]
write \(n=M(l,m)+r\) with \(0\leq r<m\). The near-boundary comparison applies unless \(l=1\) and \(m<14\). But that exceptional combination cannot occur under the hypotheses of (11): if \(l=1\) and \(m\leq13\), then
\[
M(1,m)+m=T_m+m\leq T_{13}+13=91+13=104.
\]
Thus \(n<M(1,m)+m\leq104\), contrary to the alternative assumption \(n>103\) together with integrality, which would force \(n\geq104\) and hence conflict with the strict upper bound. Therefore (16) proves (11) in this case.

It remains to consider
\[
n\geq M(l,m)+m.                                             \tag{35}
\]
Using (10) for the two adjacent layers, we have
\[
L_l(m-1,n)=L_{l+1}(m-1,n)+\frac1{l!}L_{l+1}(m-2,n-l),
\]
\[
L_l(m,n)=L_{l+1}(m,n)+\frac1{l!}L_{l+1}(m-1,n-l).             \tag{36}
\]
The two comparisons on the right involve a larger lower bound \(l+1\), hence a smaller induction parameter. Their feasibility follows from (35) and the identities
\[
M(l+1,m)=M(l,m)+m,
\qquad
M(l+1,m-1)=M(l,m)-l.
\]
Thus the induction hypothesis gives
\[
L_{l+1}(m-1,n)<L_{l+1}(m,n)
\]
and
\[
L_{l+1}(m-2,n-l)<L_{l+1}(m-1,n-l).
\]
Multiplying the second inequality by the positive number \(1/l!\), then adding, proves the desired strict inequality through (36). The layer-growth lemma is proved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Sign of an alternating sum with increasing terms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We need a simple alternating-sum fact. If
\[
0\leq f(0)<f(1)<\cdots<f(m),\qquad f(m)>0,
\]
then
\[
(-1)^m\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^jf(j)>0.                              \tag{37}
\]
For odd \(m\), pair consecutive terms as
\[
(f(0)-f(1))+(f(2)-f(3))+\cdots+(f(m-1)-f(m)),
\]
which is negative. For even \(m\), write the sum as
\[
f(0)+(f(2)-f(1))+(f(4)-f(3))+\cdots+(f(m)-f(m-1)),
\]
which is positive, and is strictly positive because the last term is present and
\(f(m)>f(m-1)\) (with the case \(m=0\) immediate). This proves (37).

Now let \(n>103\), and choose the unique \(m\) satisfying
\[
T_m\leq n<T_{m+1}.                                           \tag{38}
\]
Existence follows because the triangular numbers tend to infinity, and uniqueness from
\(T_{m+1}=T_m+m+1>T_m\). Here \(m>0\).

By (7), every layer with index greater than \(m\) vanishes, so (6) becomes
\[
[x^n]P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^jL_1(j,n).                      \tag{39}
\]
All these layers are nonnegative, and the top layer is positive by the explicit set constructed after (7). For \(j<m\), feasibility for layer \(j+1\) follows from
\[
M(1,j+1)=T_{j+1}\leq T_m\leq n.
\]
Since \(n>103\), the layer-growth lemma with \(l=1\) gives
\[
L_1(j,n)<L_1(j+1,n)\qquad(0\leq j<m).
\]
Applying (37) to (39) yields
\[
(-1)^m[x^n]P_n(x)>0.                                        \tag{40}
\]
Since \(n!>0\), we conclude
\[
(-1)^m a(n)>0\qquad\text{whenever }n>103
\text{ and }T_m\leq n<T_{m+1}.                              \tag{41}
\]
In particular, none of these coefficients is zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Consecutive coefficients and triangular endpoints
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume now that \(n>104\), and let \(m\) be determined by (38). Both \(n\) and
\(n-1\) exceed \(103\), so (41) applies to both.

If \(n>T_m\), then
\[
T_m\leq n-1<n<T_{m+1}.
\]
Thus both \(n-1\) and \(n\) lie in the same triangular interval. By (41), both
\(a(n-1)\) and \(a(n)\) have sign \((-1)^m\), and their product is positive.

If \(n=T_m\), then \(m>0\) and
\[
T_{m-1}\leq n-1<T_m,
\]
because \(T_m=T_{m-1}+m\). Therefore (41) says that \(a(n)\) has sign
\((-1)^m\), while \(a(n-1)\) has sign \((-1)^{m-1}\). These signs are opposite, so
\(a(n)a(n-1)<0\).

Consequently, for every \(n>104\),
\[
a(n)a(n-1)<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=T_m
\text{ for some }m.
\]
Together with the recurrence computation (4), which established the same equivalence for \(1\leq n\leq104\), this proves the claim for every positive integer \(n\).
